name: Vitamin K2

lead: Vitamin K2 is a group of fat-soluble compounds called menaquinones, most commonly sold as MK-4 and MK-7, found in fermented foods such as natto, some cheeses and animal products. It is popular in bone and "facial structure" supplement stacks alongside vitamin D and calcium.

Its role is to activate calcium-binding proteins including osteocalcin. Trial results on bone density and fractures are mixed, with the strongest signals coming from high-dose MK-4 studies in Japan, and no evidence that it alters facial bone in healthy adults.

paras: Vitamin K2 is a cofactor for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, which modifies osteocalcin and matrix Gla protein so they can bind calcium. Carboxylated osteocalcin helps incorporate calcium into bone matrix, and matrix Gla protein is thought to limit calcification of soft tissue such as arteries. MK-7 persists in circulation longer than MK-4.

Supplements are generally well tolerated, and no upper limit has been set. It can interfere with warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists, so people on anticoagulants should seek medical advice. Claims about cardiovascular or bone benefits are stronger in marketing than in controlled trials.
